title: What Ancient Egyptian are we learning?
objectives: Understand why Middle Egyptian is the teaching base
Separate historical pronunciation from Egyptological reading
content: This course teaches Middle Egyptian, the classical phase most often used for learning monumental hieroglyphic texts. Hieroglyphs are a writing system, not a language by themselves. Egyptian changed over millennia and was written in hieroglyphic, hieratic, demotic and later Coptic scripts. Early Egyptian writing normally omits vowels, so exact historical pronunciation is partly reconstructed rather than directly recorded.

examples.swahili: maneno ya kimungu / maandishi ya hieroglyphi

quiz.q: Do hieroglyphs represent a separate language from Egyptian?

title: The one-consonant signs
content: Uniliteral signs represent one consonant. They are the closest thing Egyptian has to an alphabet, but ordinary Egyptian spelling also uses biliterals, triliterals, logograms and determinatives.

title: Reading direction and sign orientation
content: Hieroglyphs may be written left-to-right or right-to-left and in rows or columns. Human and animal signs normally face toward the beginning of the text. Signs are aesthetically grouped into visual blocks rather than simply typed as an alphabetic line.

quiz.q: If figures face right, where do you normally begin reading?

title: Logograms, phonograms and determinatives
content: A sign can write a word directly as a logogram, contribute sounds as a phonogram, or classify meaning as a determinative. The same graphic sign can have different functions in different words. Determinatives are usually not pronounced.

title: Biliterals, triliterals and phonetic complements
content: Many signs represent two or three consonants. Scribes often add one-consonant signs after a multi-consonant sign to confirm part of its reading. These additions are phonetic complements, not repeated sounds.

quiz.q: If a triliteral is followed by a sign repeating its final consonant, should you pronounce that consonant twice?

title: Transliteration and Manuel de Codage
content: Egyptologists transliterate Egyptian consonants with symbols such as ꜣ, ꜥ, ḥ, ḫ, ẖ, š, ṯ and ḏ. Digital Manuel de Codage commonly writes these as A, a, H, x, X, S, T and D. Transliteration is not the same as reconstructed pronunciation.

quiz.q: In common MdC, D normally corresponds to which transliteration sign?

title: How Egyptologists pronounce written consonants
objectives: Avoid confusing it with historical speech
content: For convenience, Egyptologists often insert an e-like vowel between consonants when reading transliterations aloud. ꜣ and ꜥ may be given conventional vowel-like values. This is a scholarly reading convention, not a recording of exactly how Middle Egyptian sounded.

quiz.q: Is 'nefer' guaranteed to be the exact Middle Kingdom pronunciation of nfr?
